planting.note: Wait until soil is thoroughly warm and nighttime temperatures stay mild, since this long-season cushaw type needs a full, uninterrupted stretch of heat to fill out its large fruit.

directions: A long-vining cushaw-type heirloom grown in the southern Corn Belt since the early nineteenth century, producing oblong, crook-necked fruit with pale cream rind faintly striped in green and firm, dry flesh suited to pies and baking. Give the sprawling vines generous room, often trained along cornfield rows in its traditional culture, and keep moisture even through flowering and fruit set. Harvest once the rind resists a fingernail and the stem has dried, then cure in a warm spot for a week before moving fruit to cool, dry storage. Well-cured fruit keeps for months, a trait that made it a staple winter keeper long before modern butternut and cheese types became common.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the soil has warmed, since this Northern Plains heirloom was bred for a shorter continental growing season than many maxima types.

directions: Cultivated for generations by the Arikara people along the Missouri River in present-day North Dakota, this heirloom bears oblong fruit in mottled orange and green with a distinctive pale star marking the blossom end. Plants are relatively compact for a maxima squash and set two to three fruits per vine, making efficient use of a shorter northern season. The moist, sweet flesh is reminiscent of a Hubbard and works well in soups and purees. Cure harvested fruit briefly in a warm location before moving to cool storage, where it keeps remarkably well into late winter.

planting.note: Sow directly once the danger of frost has passed, as this fast-maturing heirloom was selected for a short continental summer and rewards early planting.

directions: A rare Native American heirloom preserved from the Omaha people of the Missouri Valley, bearing small cylindrical fruit typically three to five pounds with smooth tan-orange rind. It matures notably faster than most winter squash, making it well suited to gardeners with cool or short-season climates. The dense, sweet flesh is good for baking and keeps in storage for several months after curing. Because the vines are relatively modest in reach compared to many maxima types, it also suits smaller garden plots.
